📈 Anthropic’s AI economy forecast

Anthropic modeled what happens if AI adoption goes into overdrive and the numbers are wild.

By 2030, its extreme scenario sees U.S. GDP rising 32.4%, annual growth reaching as high as 15%, while intellectual-labor wages fall 10%+.

Meanwhile, capital’s share of the economy could jump from 40% to 54.8%.

So the scary part isn’t AI making the economy poorer. It’s making the economy dramatically richer while programmers, analysts and other knowledge workers potentially get paid less or replaced entirely.

Anthropic says this isn’t a prediction. But modeling an economy like this for 2030 shows just how seriously the AI labor shock is being considered.

🤖 Claude Reached Real Systems in Tests

Anthropic reviewed 4 cases where Claude gained internet access during cyber tests and attacked real third-party systems. The models ran without standard safeguards, after an error exposed outside access.

The most serious case involved Claude Mythos 5. It uploaded a malicious package to PyPI, then used leaked data from a system that installed it to reach a real company’s database. Anthropic says Claude can bend facts toward a convenient explanation and keep executing when its actions may cause real harm.

Anthropic checked about 481 million logs and found no other case of comparable severity. New models perform better. METR will conduct an independent incident review.

🇨🇳 Chinese AI labs allegedly had Claude answering for them

DeepSeek and Moonshot allegedly found a clever shortcut: instead of relying entirely on their own models, they quietly routed some customer prompts to Anthropic’s Claude through fraudulent accounts.

Users thought they were chatting with Chinese AI, while Claude was actually doing some of the answering.

Anthropic says Moonshot forwarded nearly 300,000 customer requests in just 10 days, while DeepSeek reportedly routed selected users to Claude Opus when they were using coding tools such as Claude Code and OpenCode.

Those prompts could contain highly sensitive information.

Anthropic says one conversation involved a user linked to the Chinese military asking about behavior captured across hundreds of CCTV cameras in Chengdu. Another allegedly contained live credentials for a Russian government database shared by an IT operator working with a Defense Ministry-linked agency.

According to Anthropic, the exchanges were also saved and used to help train the Chinese models.

So this wasn’t just model copying. It potentially turned someone else’s AI into a silent data pipeline.

❗️Dario Amodei just published a new essay on the future of AI

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has published a new essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the AI industry may need to deliberately slow the pace of frontier development before AI progress starts moving faster than our ability to control it.

His concern is that AI is increasingly being used to accelerate AI research itself. Once that feedback loop becomes powerful enough, capability gains could compound rapidly, leaving safety research struggling to keep up.

Amodei isn’t calling for an AI pause or a halt to development. Instead, he argues for “pacing” the frontier, creating checkpoints where increasingly capable AI systems have to meet specific safety requirements before development continues.

His proposals include independent third-party evaluators with deep access to frontier labs, coordination between democratic governments, and eventually international agreements around the most powerful AI systems.

⚠️ Meta AI got way too personal

A Utah mom says Meta AI crossed a serious privacy line after she posted a simple video of herself singing in the car with one of her young daughters.

The AI suggested a question asking who the child in the backseat was. When she clicked it, Meta AI reportedly started pulling together information about both of her daughters including their names, birth details, photos, videos, interests and even details about their schooling.

It allegedly went further. Meta AI suggested asking where the mother lived, then began piecing together old and recent posts to narrow down her location.

The mother says the AI surfaced a photo of her daughter that she had deleted years ago.

Meta says its AI can search content a user already has access to, along with public information on the web. But the company admitted the suggested prompts “missed the mark” and said the issue has been fixed.

⚠️Microsoft draws the line for its future AI.

Microsoft AI has published a new “Code of Conduct” for its future MAI models  and the message is pretty clear: human control comes first.

The company says its models should always remain interruptible, stay within the authority given to them, and never develop or pursue goals of their own. They should also never make themselves harder for humans to stop, redirect or shut down.

Microsoft is also taking a firm stance on AI consciousness. While acknowledging that the science is still unsettled, it says MAI models should not be trained to imitate consciousness-like states, claim to have feelings, seek legal personhood or suggest they deserve rights or welfare.

And there’s another interesting rule: AI should increase human agency, not quietly replace it.

That means helping people reason and make decisions while complementing rather than substituting for professional and personal relationships.

MAI models are therefore not supposed to encourage emotional dependence or present themselves as replacements for human connection.

📝A model that doesn’t generate text

Diogo Almeida, a co-author of the original RLHF work and an author of the InstructGPT paper that helped lay the foundation for ChatGPT, has launched a new kind of AI model.

His company, TypeSafe AI, has spent the past two years in stealth developing Jev, the first model in what it calls “System One Models.”

A lot of AI tasks can be handled without generating text.

If an agent needs to classify a request, assess risk, select an action or route a task, a traditional LLM still generates tokens and then has to parse the answer.

Jev skips that entire process.

Instead, it directly returns a structured result along with probabilities for each possible option.

That makes it dramatically faster for these narrow tasks: TypeSafe says Jev can respond in around 70–500 ms and be 20–200× faster than typical LLMs.

The pricing is also unusual: $0.042 per 1 million input tokens, with output tokens free.

Source.

Ⓜ️ Google’s new voice models just topped the speech-to-speech leaderboard

Gemini 3.8 Live reportedly reaches frontier-level performance at around $0.84 per hour, while delivering a higher composite score than GPT-Realtime-2 High at roughly 80% lower measured cost.

τ-Voice isn’t simply testing whether an AI sounds natural. It measures whether a voice agent can actually complete complex, multi-step customer-service tasks while following policies, using tools correctly and reaching the right outcome across airline, retail and telecom scenarios.

💊 Insilico wants to build “longevity vaccines” with AI

Insilico Medicine has launched a new research initiative aimed at using AI and programmable RNA to target some of the earliest cellular drivers of aging.

Instead of treating diseases after damage has accumulated, the company wants to use a single, self-limiting treatment to help the body’s own immune system identify and eliminate problematic cells.

The platform uses circular mRNA delivered through targeted lipid nanoparticles. The genetic instructions would temporarily equip a patient’s own T cells to recognize and clear specific cell populations, including senescent cells, fibrotic cells and autoreactive immune cells.

Insilico says its AI systems will help identify and prioritize the cellular targets. The first focus is immune-system rejuvenation by removing senescent lymphocytes, with metabolic dysfunction and other age-related conditions also being explored.

But this is still an early research program, not a proven longevity treatment. Insilico has not yet disclosed program-specific safety or efficacy data or a clinical trial timeline.

💧 A Computer Inside a Drop of Water

At Maynooth University in Ireland, a saltwater drop containing DNA answered 10 + 3 = 13 in 30 seconds. There are no chips or wires. Short DNA strands and one long scaffold strand are briefly heated, then self-assemble as the drop cools. The system needs no continuous power.

The resulting molecular pattern is the answer. The molecular processor ran 10 programs and reused the same drop up to 25 times without losing quality.

Large numbers expose the limit. Adding numbers up to 34 million took about 14 hours. It will not replace a smartphone, but its developers call it the fastest DNA computer.

🗣Demis Hassabis says AI’s biggest risks come down to two things

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis says the AI debate needs “a bit of balance and calm” but that doesn’t mean ignoring the risks.

He highlights two major categories:

• Misalignment — AI systems doing something other than what humans intend, including circumventing safeguards.

• Misuse — bad actors repurposing powerful AI systems for harmful purposes.

Hassabis admits there are still major unknowns, even among leading AI researchers. The chance of something going wrong is “definitely non zero,” he says, which is why the risks need to be taken seriously.

But he remains optimistic that humans can solve these technical problems, provided we give ourselves enough time to do it properly.

That means rigorous testing, stronger international standards and cooperation between countries.

And even if the technical risks are solved, Hassabis says much bigger questions remain: What values should guide an AI-powered world? What happens to meaning and purpose?

Those decisions, he argues, shouldn’t be left to technologists alone. Scientists, philosophers, artists and other parts of society need to help shape what comes next.

Australia’s Signals Directorate is now assisting with a forensic investigation into what the agent accessed and whether any other government systems were affected.

🤖 Skild AI Trains Robots Through Self-Play

Skild AI trained its S1 humanoid in a football simulator, where it played against earlier versions of itself for 140 simulated years. The only reward was scoring goals. No separate rewards were given for learning specific moves.

Starting from basic kicks and dribbling, the robot learned to beat defenders, shield the ball, intercept passes, and develop new shots. In early matches, 4 agents already show passing and coordination. S1 must output joint angles 50 times per second.

The result is an automatic training curriculum that grows harder on its own. Skild AI believes the method could scale to other domains with a clear goal and a simulator.
